# The map: what we know, filed by the question it answers

**Start here.** Written 2026-11-15, after the audit (`2026-11-15-audit/`), at the owner's request: "recategorize all the work … transfer what we already know into a new architecture with clear purposes and clear tests and new categories … think with your own individual opinion."

* **Every study, one by one:** [CATALOG.md](CATALOG.md) (generated by `2026-11-15-architecture/catalog.py`).
* **How we test:** [METHOD.md](METHOD.md). **The theory behind it:** [FOUNDATION.md](FOUNDATION.md). **TSLA rules:** [TSLA_PLAYBOOK.md](TSLA_PLAYBOOK.md). **Chronological log:** [INDEX.md](INDEX.md).

## Purpose
**Each day, know the market's state and what it makes likely (how big, where, how fast). Turn that into entry and exit rules for SPY and TSLA calls. Keep a live score against the options market's own odds.**

## How the work is filed
A call buyer makes money when the move that happens is bigger, sooner or more one-sided than the option charged for. That gives seven questions. All 116 pieces of work since 2026-10-02 are filed under the question they inform:

| # | Question | Items | Robust | Lean | Null | No test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How big will the next move be? | 10 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | Where does it stall, turn or speed up? | 18 | 2 | 2 | 9 | 5 |
| 3 | Which way? | 33 | 3 | 11 | 10 | 9 |
| 4 | When does it start, and how long does it last? | 15 | 0 | 6 | 5 | 4 |
| 5 | **Is the option cheap or dear for that? Which structure?** | **4** | 0 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | When to get out? | 8 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 0 |
| 7 | What breaks it? | 6 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| | Live desk, theory library, tools | 22 | | | | |

* **Each study also carries:**
  * a mechanism tag: positioning, flow and liquidity, forced flows, volatility dynamics, price history, macro;
  * an evidence grade: robust, lean, null, no test;
  * a next step: rule, refine, park, close.
* **Robust** means replicated or out-of-sample, or p ≤ 0.005 with controls. **Lean** means it passed once, partly, or on one day. Leans are not traded.

## My read, as the consultant
1. **We found the right variables and then asked the wrong follow-up.**
   * 33 studies asked "which way?" and 4 asked "is it priced?".
   * For an option buyer, knowing a move will be big is worth money only if the option's price does not already include it.
   * The founding report said so on Oct 2 (§4b: the edge moves to "realized vs implied volatility"). Its ladder table showed structure mattering more than the signal: naked calls bought on the early rungs lose, call spreads gain. We never followed that up.
2. **Stop hunting for direction.**
   * The three robust results under "which way?" are one thing: TSLA's own positioning.
   * Analogs, indicators, flows, insiders and politics produced nothing in 10 tests. More attempts will mostly produce false positives.
   * Direction comes from the trend and from your own read. Our tilts are tie-breakers.
3. **A lean is not knowledge.** About 55 tests were run. Three passes at the 5% level are expected by luck alone, and we hold 19 leans. Each one is either logged forward or given one decisive retest. None is traded.
4. **Rare setups cannot be proven by more backtests.**
   * The ladder and the full setup fire a few times a year. Re-mining the same history only overfits it.
   * Their evidence has to come from a forward log with odds stated in advance.
   * The edge lab (founding §4ad) gives the detection limits. Use it as the power check before any test.
5. **Order-flow microstructure is the most interesting line and the least likely to pay at this budget and horizon.** Run one small designed pilot, then decide.
6. **Your own trades are the best dataset we have not looked at.** If you export your fills, we can measure what costs you most: direction, the option's price, time decay or exit timing.
7. **Reading belongs to a test.** Before each step, find and read in full the papers on that exact question. No separate reading track.

## The seven questions

### 1. How big will the next move be?
* **Why it matters:** whether to own options at all, and how far out the strike can be.
* **Proven:**
  * Low S&P dealer gamma: a big move starts more often (+13 to +26 points on the odds of a big up-leg), but the downside widens too (§4d, §4j).
  * Call gamma damps the next day's range; put gamma amplifies it in SPY and QQQ (dealer-sign).
  * Big days cluster: about 9 in 10 are aftershocks (aftershocks).
  * For TSLA, use its own positioning. The S&P's gamma says nothing about it (§4k).
* **Leans:** low gamma makes the reaction to a data surprise bigger (macro-trigger).
* **Dead:** daily book-thinness proxies (liquidity-cycle).
* **Gap:** liquidity, measured directly.

### 2. Where does it stall, turn or speed up?
* **Why it matters:** strikes, targets, stops.
* **Proven:**
  * The prior day's call wall is a soft ceiling in SPY and QQQ (gamma-phase-diagram).
  * Highs and lows cluster at round numbers (positioning-tests).
* **Leans:** the pre-open flip is a weak stall level (flip-wicks).
* **Live record:** the short-gamma pocket held the Oct 30 and Nov 5 lows. The TSLA floor map failed on Nov 5.
* **Dead:** hand-drawn channels and lines (11 nulls across both eras), opens and extremes at top open-interest strikes, the put wall as a floor.
* **Open:** floors and absorption (needs trade data); TSLA's call wall (GW1) and wall size as a dose (GW2).

### 3. Which way?
* **Why it matters:** calls need direction.
* **Proven (one family):** TSLA freed → up-bursts 3.8× with controls; full setup 39% up vs 17% down within 3 sessions; own-positioning up-legs beyond luck (§4s, §4w, §4z).
* **Leans, as tie-breakers only:**
  * RSI washout in TSLA;
  * the S&P ladder's odds (65–79% vs 50–58%, with intervals overlapping the base);
  * earnings crowding (§4e);
  * closing imbalance for the last 10 minutes.
* **Dead:** year analogs, indicator regimes, option ratios and flows as forecasts, smart money and insiders, politics odds, forecasting models (Kronos, TimesFM), leveraged-ETF close flow, the SPCX lead.
* **Next:** no new predictors. Ask whether the proven tilts are already in option prices (queue steps 1–2).

### 4. When does it start, and how long does it last?
* **Why it matters:** time decay is paid daily.
* **Proven:** nothing yet.
* **Leans:**
  * the ladder leads a leg by about 5 days (§4i);
  * gamma builds into monthly expiry and resets after (§4h);
  * build-up shocks stay volatile longer (signature-test);
  * Monday up-bursts in TSLA (§4o).
* **Rule of thumb that held:** the calendar sets when things happen, not which way.
* **Dead:** the July/October pattern, speed extremes marking the low, capitulation signatures, exhaustion read from bars (failed twice), breadth at the start of a dip (failed live).
* **Open:** one free lead, ND1: in short gamma, a price low that implied volatility does not confirm.

### 5. Is the option cheap or dear for that? Which structure?
* **Why it matters:** this is where knowledge becomes money. It is the gap.
* **All we have, on rough estimates:**
  * Ladder (§4i, flat volatility): naked 60-day calls bought on the early rungs return −1% to −6%; call spreads +10% to +18%; naked calls pay only after the volatility crush (R7).
  * Gamma release + volatility crush rule (§4f): 73% hit out of sample, calls lumpy, not beyond the 95th percentile of random entries.
  * Election premium: small in SPY, present in TSLA (election-vol).
  * TSLA 5-minute breakout: +29.5 bp a day out of sample; no exit rule improves it (orb-gamma).
  * Shorting shares at the wall fails; the option version is untested (wall-short, GW5).
* **Next:** queue steps 1, 2 and 6.

### 6. When to get out?
* **Why it matters:** the owner's first stated goal (OWNER_NOTES, Oct 29).
* **Proven:**
  * Earnings-reaction gap-ups fade in the first hour, more so since 2020 (calendar-mechanics).
  * Moves made on low dealer-gamma days give back about 18% in 10 sessions; month-end and index-event moves too (forced-flow).
* **Leans:** legs end as gamma rebuilds (§4p); call-skew richening during a run (permanence).
* **Dead:** "house of cards" footprints, gap context, open-fade predictors, single top gauges for TSLA, the 09:35 rule.
* **Gap:** no exit rule has been measured in option P&L, and the owner's actual exits have not been measured at all.

### 7. What breaks it?
* **Why it matters:** one crash day can erase a month.
* **Proven:** crash days are a liquidity regime change. Normal impact cannot produce them (crash-law).
* **Leans:** SPY drags TSLA about 2× on S&P down days; momentum and RSI flag 10% corrections modestly (sp-multivariate).
* **Live record:** my adjusted odds missed Nov 5; the pocket map caught where it stopped.
* **Dead:** AAPL decoupling as a top warning, record divergence, 2000 and 2022 analogs as forecasts.
* **Gap:** a liquidity gauge, and whether it warns before the fall.

## Operating rules
1. **Three lanes, never mixed:** desk (the daily card), test (one at a time), build.
2. **A gate before every test:**
   * which of the seven questions it serves;
   * which decision it changes;
   * whether the test has the power to see the effect.
3. **Look first:** 5–10 individual cases before any statistics. No pooling across regimes or eras.
4. **Fix the rules before running.** Report in odds, levels and option P&L.
5. **One home for conclusions:** a line in this map and in the catalog. Otherwise it does not exist.
6. **Every forward call** has a probability and a due date, and is scored against the market's odds.
7. **Weekly review:** the scoreboard, what moved in the map, and one question for next week.
